## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Deep Learning for Image Restoration and Synthesis
  Official title       Apprentissage Profond pour la Restauration et la Synthese d’Images
  Instructors          A. ALMANSA, S. LADJAL, A. NEWSON (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 2 · period 2 (04/01/2027 – 02/04/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 36 h (lectures 24 h, labs 12 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Image processing
  Language             English or French, according to the preferences of the audience (master-mva.com)
  Assessment           Individual lab reports, and an individual project with a report and an oral defence at the end of the course (master-mva.com); “partial continuous assessment” (Université Paris-Saclay); no weights displayed
  Prerequisites        Applied mathematics (linear algebra, numerical analysis, differential calculus, Fourier analysis) and programming (Python, Matlab); basic notions of image processing, optimisation and deep learning are useful but are introduced in the course (master-mva.com)
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has met convolution and gradient descent, and wants to understand when a neural network really improves an image and when it only seems to.

**Empirical first**: a network trained to super-resolve images that were downsampled with the bicubic kernel looks excellent on its benchmark, then produces ringing and hallucinated textures on a real camera image, whose blur is different. A denoiser trained with the squared loss returns images that are visibly too smooth, even though its PSNR is the best available.

This course studies image models: the assumptions on natural images that turn an ill-posed restoration problem into a solvable one, and that let a machine synthesise new images. Deep learning is presented as the latest of these models, side by side with the variational and statistical models that preceded it, on denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, texture synthesis and image generation. It builds on [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Image Denoising: the Human–Machine Competition](../s1-image-denoising/index.html) and [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), and it runs alongside [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) and [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Write a restoration task (denoising, deblurring, super-resolution, inpainting) as a forward model and diagnose its ill-posedness in the Fourier domain.
-   Derive the Wiener filter, the Tikhonov and total-variation estimators, and wavelet shrinkage, and say which image model each one encodes.
-   Train a convolutional denoiser or super-resolution network, choose its loss, and predict what that loss does to the output (posterior mean, median, blur).
-   Prove that training on pairs of noisy images (Noise2Noise) has the same minimiser as training on clean targets.
-   Solve a linear inverse problem with plug-and-play ADMM, prove its fixed-point convergence under the bounded-denoiser assumption, and relate a denoiser to the score through Tweedie's formula.
-   Synthesise textures with random phase noise, with Gram-matrix statistics of a convolutional network, and with a spectrum constraint.
-   Derive the evidence lower bound, implement a variational autoencoder, and explain why its samples are blurry.
-   Derive the optimal discriminator of a GAN, relate the GAN game to the Jensen–Shannon and Wasserstein distances, and train a WGAN-GP.
-   State and prove the perception–distortion trade-off, and evaluate a restoration method with distortion and perceptual metrics without falling into their classical traps.
-   Sample from a posterior with a diffusion model or with Langevin dynamics driven by a denoiser, and say what can go wrong.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com starts from an observation: smaller sensors and larger computing power have made images ubiquitous, but those images need more and more demanding post-processing (filtering, restoration) to reach good quality. At the heart of such processing lie image models, which make efficient algorithms possible, and deep learning is the most recent of a long list of them.

The stated goal is to put recent deep-learning techniques for image quality in perspective with the methods that existed before them. The course explores denoising, super-resolution, deblurring, texture synthesis and the generation of natural images, presents the strengths and limitations of each technique, and analyses the methods critically, sometimes showing the pitfalls into which they fell.

The description lists five themes, each made of a lecture and a lab, and announces 8 sessions of 3 h (lecture and lab), 2 revision sessions and 1 project-presentation session, on Tuesday afternoons at Télécom Paris. The Université Paris-Saclay programme table gives 24 h of lectures and 12 h of labs, under partial continuous assessment. Every item is matched below.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites (master-mva.com): applied mathematics (linear algebra, numerical analysis, differential calculus, Fourier analysis) and programming (Python, Matlab). Basic notions of image processing, optimisation and deep learning are useful, but the course introduces them; ch. 0 reviews what is needed.

-   **Refreshers** — [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (SVD, gradients, convexity), [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (conditional expectation, Gaussian vectors, Bayes), [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (every lab).
-   **First-semester courses that prepare it** — [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html), [Image Denoising: the Human–Machine Competition](../s1-image-denoising/index.html), [Convex Optimization](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html) (proximal operators, ADMM), [Introduction to Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (variational inference), [Sub-Pixel Image Processing](../s1-sub-pixel-image-processing/index.html) (sampling, aliasing), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html) (Langevin, MCMC), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein distance), [Stochastic Calculus in Machine Learning](../s1-stochastic-calculus-ml/index.html) (diffusion processes).
-   **Related second-semester courses** — [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html), [Inverse Problems and Imaging](../s2-inverse-problems-imaging/index.html), [Diffusion and Multiscale Models in Artificial Intelligence](../s2-diffusion-multiscale/index.html), [Deep Learning in Practice](../s2-deep-learning-in-practice/index.html), [Deep Learning for Medical Imaging](../s2-deep-learning-medical-imaging/index.html), [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Remote Sensing Data](../s2-remote-sensing/index.html).
-   **Afterwards** — the [Research Internship](../s3-research-internship/index.html): restoration and generative modelling are frequent internship subjects in imaging laboratories and companies.

### Course outline

-   **Review: images, Fourier analysis, estimation and network training** — the discrete Fourier transform, the convolution theorem, aliasing, the MMSE and MAP estimators, and convolutional layers.
-   **Image degradations and classical image models** — forward models, quality metrics, Wiener, Tikhonov, total variation, wavelet shrinkage and patch models.
-   **End-to-end deep learning for denoising and super-resolution** — supervised restoration, what the loss estimates, DnCNN, Noise2Noise, SRCNN, sub-pixel convolution and the pitfalls of synthetic training data.
-   **Inverse problems: variational, statistical and hybrid methods** — MAP and MMSE, proximal splitting, plug-and-play ADMM and its convergence, Tweedie's formula, RED and unrolled networks.
-   **Generative models for texture synthesis** — random phase noise, Gram matrices of convolutional features, the spectrum constraint and feed-forward texture networks.
-   **Autoencoders and variational autoencoders** — linear autoencoders and PCA, the evidence lower bound, the reparameterisation trick and the limits of VAEs.
-   **Generative adversarial networks** — the minimax game, the Jensen–Shannon and Wasserstein distances, conditional GANs for restoration and the evaluation of generators.
-   **Perception, distortion and the critical evaluation of restoration** — why no estimator can be both accurate and realistic, and how metrics mislead.
-   **Diffusion models and generative priors for inverse problems** — denoising score matching, DDPM, and posterior sampling with Langevin dynamics and diffusion guidance.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — convergent plug-and-play, uncertainty, self-supervision, memorisation (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session even if you know the material: the convolution theorem, aliasing and the MMSE estimator are used in every later chapter without warning.
-   After each session, run the code block of the chapter, change one parameter (noise level, blur width, loss, regularisation weight) and predict the effect before looking.
-   Do the exercises listed in the *Practice* column right after the session; the ★ ones check the session, the ★★ ones prepare the next.
-   Keep a lab notebook: the official assessment includes individual lab reports, and the labs of sessions 2–10 are where they come from.
-   Read ch. 7 twice, once after ch. 2 and once after ch. 6: it is the critical lens the course description asks for.
-   Environment: Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn (its two bundled sample images and the digits data set) and PyTorch on CPU; every code block runs in well under a minute on a laptop.

## 0. Review: images, Fourier analysis, estimation and network training {#ch0}

Restoration and synthesis keep manipulating three objects: the image as an array of numbers, the convolution that models a blur and builds a network, and the conditional distribution of the clean image given what was observed. This chapter reviews the M1 facts about them that later chapters use without proof.

### 0.1 Discrete images and the Fourier transform

A grey-level image is an array $u \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$. We index it by $x \in \Omega = \{0, \dots, n-1\}^2$ and read indices modulo $n$: the image is extended periodically. This convention makes every formula below exact; real boundaries are handled by symmetric extension or by cropping.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Two-dimensional discrete Fourier transform]{.tag} The DFT of $u$ is
$$
\hat u(\omega) = \sum_{x \in \Omega} u(x)\, e^{-2i\pi \langle \omega, x \rangle / n}, \qquad \omega \in \Omega,
$$
and it is inverted by
$$
u(x) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \hat u(\omega)\, e^{2i\pi \langle \omega, x \rangle / n}.
$$

Parseval's identity reads $\sum_x |u(x)|^2 = n^{-2} \sum_\omega |\hat u(\omega)|^2$. Frequencies are often written in cycles per pixel, $\omega / n \in [-\tfrac12, \tfrac12)^2$.
:::

The *circular convolution* of a kernel $k$ and an image $u$ is
$$
(k * u)(x) = \sum_{y \in \Omega} k(y)\, u(x - y).
$$

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Convolution theorem]{.tag} For all $k, u \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$,
$$
\widehat{k * u}(\omega) = \hat k(\omega)\, \hat u(\omega) \quad \text{for every } \omega \in \Omega.
$$

::: proof
Write the definition and exchange the sums:
$$
\widehat{k * u}(\omega) = \sum_{y} k(y) \sum_{x} u(x - y)\, e^{-2i\pi \langle \omega, x \rangle / n}.
$$

In the inner sum substitute $z = x - y$, a bijection of $\Omega$ modulo $n$, and split the exponential into a factor in $y$ and a factor in $z$. The inner sum becomes
$$
e^{-2i\pi \langle \omega, y \rangle / n}\, \hat u(\omega),
$$
and the outer sum then gives $\hat k(\omega)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A convolution is therefore *diagonal in the Fourier basis*: its eigenvalues are the values of the transfer function $\hat k(\omega)$. It is invertible exactly when $\hat k$ never vanishes, and its condition number is the ratio of the largest to the smallest value of $|\hat k|$. This single fact explains why deblurring is unstable (ch. 1) and why every deconvolution algorithm in this course works in the Fourier domain.

### 0.2 Sampling and aliasing

Super-resolution undoes a subsampling, so we need to know exactly what subsampling does to frequencies. One dimension is enough to see it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Aliasing]{.tag} Let $u \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n$ even, and keep one sample out of two: $v(m) = u(2m)$ for $0 \le m < n/2$. Then, for $0 \le k < n/2$,
$$
\hat v(k) = \tfrac12 \big( \hat u(k) + \hat u(k + n/2) \big).
$$

::: proof
The quantity $\tfrac12 (1 + (-1)^x)$ equals $1$ when $x$ is even and $0$ otherwise, and $(-1)^x = e^{-2i\pi (n/2) x / n}$. Hence
$$
\hat v(k) = \sum_{x} u(x)\, \tfrac12 \big(1 + e^{-2i\pi (n/2) x / n}\big)\, e^{-2i\pi k x / n},
$$
which is half the sum of the DFTs of $u$ at $k$ and at $k + n/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Frequencies $k$ and $k + n/2$ fold onto each other. A high frequency of $u$ thus masquerades as a low frequency of $v$, unless $u$ was low-pass filtered before sampling, as the Shannon–Nyquist theorem requires.

Single-image super-resolution has to undo this folding. The aliased part of the low-resolution image carries information about high frequencies, which is what makes the problem solvable at all; but each low frequency mixes two unknowns, which is what makes it ill-posed.

::: ex
[Example 0.4 — A cosine that changes frequency]{.tag} Sample the cosine $\cos(2\pi \cdot 0.4\, m)$ on 250 pixels and keep one sample out of two. In units of the new sampling step its frequency is $0.8$ cycles per sample, above the Nyquist limit $0.5$. The code below finds the peak of the spectrum of the subsampled signal at

$$0.8 \text{ folded to } 1 - 0.8 = 0.2 \text{ cycles per sample.}$$
:::

### 0.3 Estimators: MMSE and MAP

In restoration the clean image $X$ is unknown and modelled as random; the observation $Y$ is a degraded version of it. An *estimator* is a function $f(Y)$. Two choices recur in every chapter.

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.5 — The MMSE estimator is the conditional mean]{.tag} If $\mathbb{E}\|X\|^2 < \infty$, then among all measurable functions $f$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|X - f(Y)\|^2 \ \ge\ \mathbb{E}\, \|X - m(Y)\|^2, \qquad m(Y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y],
$$
with equality if and only if $f(Y) = m(Y)$ almost surely. The minimum value, the *MMSE*, equals $\mathbb{E}\, \mathrm{tr}\, \mathrm{Cov}(X \mid Y)$.

::: proof
Decompose $X - f(Y) = (X - m(Y)) + (m(Y) - f(Y))$ and expand the square.

The cross term is $2\,\mathbb{E} \langle X - m(Y),\, m(Y) - f(Y) \rangle$. Conditioning on $Y$, the second factor is fixed and the first has conditional mean zero, so the cross term vanishes by the tower property.

What remains is $\mathbb{E}\|X - m(Y)\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|m(Y) - f(Y)\|^2$, and the second term is non-negative and zero only when $f(Y) = m(Y)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 0.6 — MAP estimator and the variational form]{.tag} If $X$ has a prior density $p(x) \propto e^{-\varphi(x)}$ and $Y = AX + N$ with $N \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$, the *maximum a posteriori* estimator maximises the posterior density, that is

$$
\hat x_{\mathrm{MAP}}(y) = \arg\min_x\ \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \|Ax - y\|^2 + \varphi(x).
$$

It is a variational problem: a data-fidelity term plus a regulariser. This identity is the bridge between the "variational" and the "statistical" methods of the official theme 2.
:::

The two estimators coincide for a Gaussian posterior, whose mode is its mean. They differ as soon as the prior is not Gaussian: the MAP picks the most likely image, the MMSE averages all plausible ones. Chapters 3 and 7 return to this difference, which is at the heart of the course.

### 0.4 Convolutional networks and their training

::: def
[Definition 0.7 — Convolutional layer]{.tag} A layer maps $C_{\mathrm{in}}$ input channels $h_c$ to $C_{\mathrm{out}}$ output channels by
$$
h'_{c'} = \sigma\Big( \sum_{c=1}^{C_{\mathrm{in}}} w_{c', c} * h_c + b_{c'} \Big),
$$
where each $w_{c',c}$ is an $s \times s$ kernel and $\sigma$ is a pointwise non-linearity such as $\mathrm{ReLU}(t) = \max(t, 0)$. It has $C_{\mathrm{in}} C_{\mathrm{out}} s^2$ weights and $C_{\mathrm{out}}$ biases, whatever the size of the image.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.8 — Translation equivariance]{.tag} Let $\tau_a u(x) = u(x - a)$. With periodic boundary conditions, a convolution satisfies $w * \tau_a u = \tau_a (w * u)$, and a pointwise non-linearity commutes with $\tau_a$. Hence a network $\Phi$ made only of such layers satisfies
$$
\Phi(\tau_a u) = \tau_a\, \Phi(u) \quad \text{for every translation } a.
$$

::: proof
$(w * \tau_a u)(x) = \sum_y w(y)\, u(x - y - a) = (w * u)(x - a)$. Composition preserves the property. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Equivariance is the reason why convolutional networks suit restoration: the same local rule is applied everywhere, and a network trained on small patches can be applied to a whole image. Stacking $L$ layers of $s \times s$ kernels gives a *receptive field* of $(L(s-1) + 1)^2$ pixels; for instance 17 layers of $3 \times 3$ kernels see a $35 \times 35$ neighbourhood.

Training minimises an empirical risk by stochastic gradient methods (Adam in all the labs). Backpropagation computes the gradient by the chain rule in reverse order, for a small multiple of the cost of the forward pass. Two architectural devices make deep networks trainable: residual connections, which let a block learn a correction to the identity, and batch normalisation, which standardises activations over the mini-batch.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.ndimage import convolve

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.random((64, 64))                                  # a random 64 x 64 "image"
box = np.ones((3, 3)) / 9                                 # 3 x 3 box blur
k = np.zeros((64, 64)); k[:3, :3] = box
k = np.roll(k, (-1, -1), axis=(0, 1))                     # centre the kernel at pixel (0, 0)
y_fourier = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(x) * np.fft.fft2(k)))
y_direct = convolve(x, box, mode="wrap")                  # periodic boundary conditions
print("max |Fourier - direct| =", np.abs(y_fourier - y_direct).max())

# Aliasing: a cosine at 0.4 cycles/pixel, keep one sample out of two
n = np.arange(250)
s = np.cos(2 * np.pi * 0.4 * n)
sub = s[::2]                                              # 125 samples, new sampling step = 2 pixels
peak = np.argmax(np.abs(np.fft.rfft(sub))) / len(sub)     # dominant frequency, cycles per new sample
print("frequency after subsampling:", peak, "cycles/sample (0.8 folds back to 0.2)")
```

The first line prints an error of order $10^{-16}$ (Theorem 0.2 holds to machine precision); the second prints the folded frequency $0.2$ of Example 0.4.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 0
:::

-   Convolutions are diagonal in the Fourier basis; their eigenvalues are the values of the transfer function.
-   Subsampling folds frequency $k + n/2$ onto $k$: super-resolution must unfold it.
-   The squared loss is minimised by the conditional mean; the MAP estimator is a variational problem with the negative log-prior as regulariser.
-   Convolutional networks are translation-equivariant and have a receptive field that grows linearly with depth.
::::

## 1. Image degradations and classical image models {#ch1}

Before any learning, a restoration problem is a forward model plus an image model. This chapter writes the forward models of the course, shows why inverting them naively fails, and reviews the image models that solved them before deep learning: they remain the baselines, and the building blocks of the hybrid methods of ch. 3.

### 1.1 Forward models and ill-posedness

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Linear degradation model]{.tag} The observation is
$$
y = A x + n, \qquad n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),
$$
with a known linear operator $A$. The four problems of the course are:

-   **denoising**: $A = I$;
-   **deblurring**: $A x = k * x$ for a blur kernel $k$ (defocus, motion, atmosphere);
-   **super-resolution** by a factor $s$: $A x = (k * x)\!\downarrow_s$, a blur followed by keeping one pixel out of $s$ in each direction;
-   **inpainting**: $A$ multiplies by a binary mask of known pixels.
:::

Real noise is often not Gaussian. Photon counting gives Poisson noise, whose variance grows with the intensity, and the processing chain of a camera (demosaicking, compression) correlates it in space. Gaussian white noise remains the standard model for theory and for synthetic benchmarks; ch. 2.6 discusses the price of that convention.

A problem is *well-posed* in Hadamard's sense when a solution exists, is unique and depends continuously on the data. Super-resolution and inpainting break uniqueness, since $A$ has a large kernel. Deblurring breaks stability, as the next proposition quantifies.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Noise amplification by the inverse filter]{.tag} Let $A$ be a circular convolution whose transfer function $\hat k$ never vanishes, and let $\tilde x = A^{-1} y$. Then $\tilde x - x = A^{-1} n$ and
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|\tilde x - x\|^2 = \sigma^2 \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \frac{1}{|\hat k(\omega)|^2}.
$$

::: proof
By Theorem 0.2, $A = F^{*} \mathrm{diag}(\hat k) F$ with $F$ the unitary DFT (the DFT divided by $n$). Then $A^{-1} n = F^{*} \mathrm{diag}(1/\hat k) F n$.

The noise has covariance $\sigma^2 I$ and $F$ is unitary, so $Fn$ has covariance $F (\sigma^2 I) F^{*} = \sigma^2 I$: every coordinate satisfies $\mathbb{E}|(Fn)(\omega)|^2 = \sigma^2$. Each coordinate is multiplied by $1/\hat k(\omega)$, and $F^{*}$ preserves the norm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A Gaussian blur of standard deviation $b$ pixels has transfer function
$$
\hat k(\omega) = \exp\!\big(-2\pi^2 b^2 |\xi|^2\big), \qquad \xi = \omega / n \text{ in cycles per pixel}.
$$
For $b = 2$, at the corner frequency $\xi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, this is about $7 \times 10^{-18}$. A noise of standard deviation $0.01$ is multiplied by about $10^{17}$ there: the inverse filter is useless, as Example 1.6 shows.

### 1.2 Measuring quality

::: def
[Definition 1.3 — PSNR and SSIM]{.tag} For images with values in $[0, 1]$, the *peak signal-to-noise ratio* in decibels is
$$
\mathrm{PSNR}(\hat x, x) = 10 \log_{10} \frac{1}{\mathrm{MSE}(\hat x, x)}, \qquad \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{|\Omega|} \|\hat x - x\|^2 .
$$

The *structural similarity* index (Wang, Bovik, Sheikh and Simoncelli, 2004) compares local means $\mu$, variances $\sigma^2$ and the covariance $\sigma_{uv}$ in a sliding window,
$$
\mathrm{SSIM}(u, v) = \frac{(2\mu_u \mu_v + c_1)(2\sigma_{uv} + c_2)}{(\mu_u^2 + \mu_v^2 + c_1)(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma_v^2 + c_2)},
$$
averaged over windows, with small constants $c_1, c_2$ for stability.
:::

Adding Gaussian noise of standard deviation $25/255$ to an image in $[0,1]$ gives an MSE of about $0.0096$, hence

$$\mathrm{PSNR} = 10 \log_{10}(255^2/25^2) \approx 20.17 \text{ dB}.$$

PSNR is a decreasing function of the MSE, so maximising the expected PSNR is close to computing the MMSE estimator of Theorem 0.5. Chapter 7 explains why the image with the best PSNR is rarely the one that looks best.

### 1.3 Linear estimators: Wiener and Tikhonov

The oldest image model is Gaussian: the image is a stationary Gaussian random field, entirely described by its power spectrum. Under this model the best estimator is linear.

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.4 — Wiener filter]{.tag} Work with the unitary DFT for the images; $\hat k$ remains the transfer function of the blur. Let $X$ be a centred, circularly stationary Gaussian field with power spectrum $S(\omega) = \mathbb{E}|\hat X(\omega)|^2$, and let $Y = k * X + N$ with $N$ white, of variance $\sigma^2$, independent of $X$. Then the MMSE estimator is the Fourier multiplier
$$
\widehat{\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]}(\omega) = \frac{\overline{\hat k(\omega)}\, S(\omega)}{|\hat k(\omega)|^2 S(\omega) + \sigma^2}\ \hat Y(\omega).
$$

::: proof
Circular stationarity makes the covariance of $X$ a circulant matrix, diagonal in the Fourier basis. The coefficients $\hat X(\omega)$ are therefore uncorrelated across frequencies (up to the Hermitian pairing $\omega \leftrightarrow -\omega$), and so are the $\hat N(\omega)$.

By Theorem 0.2, $\hat Y = \hat k \hat X + \hat N$ frequency by frequency. All variables are jointly Gaussian, so uncorrelated means independent, and $\mathbb{E}[\hat X(\omega) \mid Y]$ only depends on $\hat Y(\omega)$.

For jointly Gaussian centred scalars, the conditional mean is
$$
\mathbb{E}[\hat X \mid \hat Y] = \mathrm{Cov}(\hat X, \hat Y)\, \mathrm{Var}(\hat Y)^{-1}\, \hat Y .
$$
Here the covariance is $\overline{\hat k} S$ and the variance is $|\hat k|^2 S + \sigma^2$. Theorem 0.5 identifies this conditional mean as the MMSE estimator. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The Wiener gain interpolates between two regimes. Where the signal dominates the noise, it is close to the inverse filter $1/\hat k$. Where $|\hat k|^2 S$ is much smaller than $\sigma^2$, it is close to $0$: frequencies drowned in noise are discarded instead of amplified.

::: def
[Definition 1.5 — Tikhonov regularisation]{.tag} The Tikhonov estimator solves
$$
\hat x_\lambda = \arg\min_x\ \|k * x - y\|^2 + \lambda\, \|\nabla x\|^2 .
$$

With periodic finite differences its solution is the Fourier multiplier
$$
\hat x_\lambda(\omega) = \frac{\overline{\hat k(\omega)}\, \hat y(\omega)}{|\hat k(\omega)|^2 + \lambda\, |\hat d(\omega)|^2}, \qquad |\hat d(\omega)|^2 = 4 \sin^2 \tfrac{\pi \omega_1}{n} + 4 \sin^2 \tfrac{\pi \omega_2}{n}.
$$
:::

Comparing the two formulas, Tikhonov is the Wiener filter for the power spectrum $S \propto 1/|\hat d|^2$, which decays like $|\xi|^{-2}$. Natural images have power spectra that decay roughly in this way (Field, 1987), which is why this crude model works at all; it is the MAP and the MMSE estimator under that Gaussian prior.

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — Deconvolving a photograph]{.tag} Take a $256 \times 256$ grey crop of the image `china.jpg` bundled with scikit-learn, blur it with a Gaussian of standard deviation 2 pixels and add noise of standard deviation $0.01$. The code below gives the following PSNRs:

-   blurred image: 19.73 dB;
-   inverse filter: −266 dB, the noise amplification of Proposition 1.2;
-   Tikhonov with $\lambda = 10^{-2}$, the best of a grid: 20.74 dB;
-   Wiener with the *oracle* spectrum of the clean image: 21.04 dB.

Even with an oracle the gain stays near 1.3 dB: a Gaussian model cannot restore edges, which carry most of the detail.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)[100:356, 200:456] / 255.0   # 256 x 256 grey crop
n = x.shape[0]
f = np.fft.fftfreq(n)
r2 = f[:, None] ** 2 + f[None, :] ** 2
K = np.exp(-2 * np.pi ** 2 * 2.0 ** 2 * r2)          # transfer function of a Gaussian blur, std 2 px
sigma = 0.01
y = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(K * np.fft.fft2(x))) + sigma * rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
Y = np.fft.fft2(y)
psnr = lambda u: 10 * np.log10(1.0 / np.mean((u - x) ** 2))

inverse = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(Y / K))                # naive inversion: divides the noise by tiny K
L = 4 * np.sin(np.pi * f[:, None]) ** 2 + 4 * np.sin(np.pi * f[None, :]) ** 2   # |DFT of the Laplacian|
tikhonov = lambda lam: np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.conj(K) * Y / (np.abs(K) ** 2 + lam * L)))
best_lam = max([1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-1], key=lambda lam: psnr(tikhonov(lam)))
S = np.abs(np.fft.fft2(x - x.mean())) ** 2 / x.size   # oracle power spectrum (unitary DFT)
S[0, 0] = 1e6                                         # the mean is known exactly
wiener = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.conj(K) * S * Y / (np.abs(K) ** 2 * S + sigma ** 2)))
print(f"blurred {psnr(y):.2f} dB | inverse filter {psnr(inverse):.2f} dB | "
      f"Tikhonov (lambda={best_lam:g}) {psnr(tikhonov(best_lam)):.2f} dB | oracle Wiener {psnr(wiener):.2f} dB")
```

### 1.4 Edges and sparsity: total variation and wavelets

A linear estimator applies the same gain to a frequency in every image, so it cannot keep an edge sharp while smoothing a flat region. The next models are non-linear.

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Total variation and the ROF model]{.tag} The discrete isotropic total variation is
$$
\mathrm{TV}(x) = \sum_{p \in \Omega} |\nabla x(p)|, \qquad |\nabla x(p)| = \sqrt{(\partial_1 x)^2 + (\partial_2 x)^2}\,(p),
$$
with forward differences. The Rudin–Osher–Fatemi denoiser (1992) is
$$
\hat x = \arg\min_x\ \tfrac12 \|x - y\|^2 + \lambda\, \mathrm{TV}(x).
$$
:::

The problem is convex but not smooth. Chambolle's algorithm (2004) solves it through its dual, a projected gradient on vector fields of norm at most 1; the primal–dual algorithm of Chambolle and Pock (2011) handles a general operator $A$. TV keeps edges because it penalises a jump by its height, not by its square, but it favours piecewise-constant images: flat "staircases" appear in smooth gradients.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Soft thresholding]{.tag} For $\lambda > 0$ and $y \in \mathbb{R}$,
$$
\arg\min_{x \in \mathbb{R}}\ \tfrac12 (x - y)^2 + \lambda |x| = \mathrm{sign}(y)\, \max(|y| - \lambda, 0).
$$
If $W$ is an orthonormal transform, the solution of $\min_x \tfrac12 \|x - y\|^2 + \lambda \|W x\|_1$ is $W^\top$ applied to the soft thresholding of $W y$, coordinate by coordinate.

::: proof
The objective is strictly convex. If $x > 0$ is optimal, the derivative $x - y + \lambda$ vanishes, so $x = y - \lambda$, which requires $y > \lambda$; symmetrically for $x < 0$.

Otherwise $x = 0$, whose optimality condition $0 \in -y + \lambda [-1, 1]$ means $|y| \le \lambda$.

For the second claim, orthonormality gives $\|x - y\| = \|Wx - Wy\|$, so the problem separates into scalar problems on the coefficients $c = Wx$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

In a wavelet basis, natural images are *sparse*: few coefficients are large. Thresholding wavelet coefficients, with the universal threshold $\sigma \sqrt{2 \log N}$ of Donoho and Johnstone (1994) for $N$ coefficients, denoises while keeping the large coefficients that encode edges. Proposition 1.8 is also the MAP estimator of Definition 0.6 under a Laplace prior on the coefficients, a first example of a *proximal operator* (ch. 3).

### 1.5 Patches, self-similarity and a long list of image models

Natural images repeat themselves: a patch of an edge or a texture has many similar patches elsewhere in the image. *Non-local means* (Buades, Coll and Morel, 2005) replaces each pixel by an average of pixels whose surrounding patches look alike,
$$
\mathrm{NLM}(y)(p) = \frac{\sum_q w(p, q)\, y(q)}{\sum_q w(p, q)}, \qquad w(p, q) = \exp\!\Big(-\frac{\|P_p y - P_q y\|^2}{h^2}\Big),
$$
where $P_p y$ is the patch centred at $p$.

BM3D (Dabov, Foi, Katkovnik and Egiazarian, 2007) stacks similar patches into 3-D groups and shrinks them jointly in a transform domain; it was the reference Gaussian denoiser for a decade. EPLL (Zoran and Weiss, 2011) learns a Gaussian mixture model of patches from data and uses it as a prior inside a MAP, already a *learned* image model.

| Image model | Typical estimator | Era |
|---|---|---|
| Stationary Gaussian field | Wiener filter | 1940s |
| Smoothness | Tikhonov regularisation | 1960s |
| Bounded variation | ROF, TV deblurring | 1990s |
| Sparsity in a wavelet basis | Soft thresholding | 1990s |
| Self-similarity of patches | Non-local means, BM3D | 2000s |
| Learned patch mixtures | EPLL | 2010s |
| Convolutional networks | DnCNN, SRCNN (ch. 2), plug-and-play (ch. 3) | 2010s |
| Deep generative models | VAEs, GANs, diffusion (ch. 5, 6, 8) | 2010s–2020s |

The course description calls deep learning "the latest in a long list of image models". The table is that list. Every line has strengths that the next one lacks, which is why the hybrid methods of ch. 3 combine them.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 1
:::

-   Restoration problems are $y = Ax + n$; deblurring is unstable, super-resolution and inpainting are non-unique.
-   PSNR is a monotone function of the MSE; it rewards the conditional mean.
-   Wiener and Tikhonov are optimal for Gaussian image models and cannot keep edges.
-   TV and wavelet thresholding are non-linear, edge-preserving, and are MAP estimators under non-Gaussian priors.
-   Patch-based models (NL-means, BM3D, EPLL) exploit self-similarity and were the state of the art just before deep learning.
::::

## 2. End-to-end deep learning for denoising and super-resolution {#ch2}

Chapter 1 wrote the image model by hand. The end-to-end approach of the official theme 1 skips the model: it collects pairs of clean and degraded images and trains a network to map one to the other. This chapter says what such a network estimates, how the classical architectures are built, and where the approach breaks.

### 2.1 Supervised restoration and what the loss estimates

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Supervised restoration]{.tag} Given pairs $(x_i, y_i)_{i \le N}$, where $y_i$ is a degraded version of $x_i$, a network $f_\theta$ is trained by minimising the empirical risk
$$
\widehat{R}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell\big(f_\theta(y_i), x_i\big).
$$
The pairs are almost always *synthetic*: clean images degraded by an assumed forward model (Definition 1.1).
:::

With enough data and capacity, the network approaches the minimiser of the population risk over all functions. That minimiser depends on the loss, and it is not "the clean image".

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.2 — What the loss estimates]{.tag} Over all measurable functions $f$:

-   with the squared loss, the risk is minimised by the posterior mean, $f^\star(y) = \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y]$;
-   with the absolute loss on each pixel, it is minimised by the pixelwise posterior median: $f^\star(y)_p$ is a median of the law of $X_p$ given $Y = y$.

::: proof
The first claim is Theorem 0.5. For the second, the risk separates over pixels and, conditionally on $Y = y$, we minimise $c \mapsto \mathbb{E}[|X_p - c| \mid y]$.

This convex function has right derivative $P(X_p \le c \mid y) - P(X_p > c \mid y)$. It is non-negative exactly from the median on, so the minimum is reached at a median. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

When several clean images are compatible with $y$, both estimators *average* them in some sense. The averaging is invisible on smooth regions and destructive on details whose position or phase is uncertain.

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — The posterior mean erases an unobservable texture]{.tag} Let the clean signal be $X(p) = \cos(2\pi \xi p + \Phi)$, with a phase $\Phi$ uniform on $[0, 2\pi)$ and $\xi$ above the Nyquist frequency of a low-resolution observation $Y$.

Assume the camera applies an ideal low-pass filter that removes $\xi$ before subsampling. Then $Y$ carries no information on $\Phi$, which is independent of $Y$. Without that filter, $\xi$ would fold onto a low frequency (Proposition 0.3) and the phase would be observable.

Then for every pixel

$$
\mathbb{E}[X(p) \mid Y] = \mathbb{E}[\cos(2\pi \xi p + \Phi)] = 0 .
$$

The MMSE super-resolution of a fine texture is a flat region. Every plausible answer is sharp, yet their average is blurred.
:::

### 2.2 Residual learning: DnCNN

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — DnCNN (Zhang, Zuo, Chen, Meng and Zhang, 2017)]{.tag} A stack of $D$ convolutional layers of $3 \times 3$ kernels with 64 channels, batch normalisation and ReLU, whose output $R_\theta(y)$ estimates the *noise*. The denoised image is
$$
f_\theta(y) = y - R_\theta(y), \qquad \text{trained with } \ \|R_\theta(y) - (y - x)\|^2 .
$$
The paper uses $D = 17$ (a $35 \times 35$ receptive field) for a known noise level, and $D = 20$ for a single "blind" model trained over a range of levels.
:::

Learning the residual instead of the image has two justifications. At initialisation the residual branch is small and the network is close to the identity, a good starting point for a mild degradation. And the noise is a simpler target than the image: it has no structure for Gaussian noise. FFDNet (Zhang, Zuo and Zhang, 2018) adds the noise level as an input map, so one network handles any level, even varying in space.

The code below trains a four-layer version on random patches of one photograph and tests it on another. After less than a minute of training on a CPU it reaches 27.28 dB, against 20.17 dB for the noisy image and 26.50 dB for the best Gaussian filter. Exercise 14 plugs it into the algorithm of ch. 3.

```python
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image
from scipy.ndimage import gaussian_filter

torch.manual_seed(0); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
gray = lambda im: im.astype(np.float32).mean(axis=2) / 255.0
train = gray(load_sample_image("china.jpg"))                     # training image
test = gray(load_sample_image("flower.jpg"))[100:356, 200:456]   # a different image for testing
sigma = 25 / 255

body = nn.Sequential(                                            # small DnCNN-like residual network
    nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Conv2d(32, 1, 3, padding=1))
denoise = lambda y: y - body(y)                                  # the network predicts the noise
opt = torch.optim.Adam(body.parameters(), lr=2e-3)
for it in range(800):                                            # random 24 x 24 patches, fresh noise
    i, j = rng.integers(0, train.shape[0] - 24, 16), rng.integers(0, train.shape[1] - 24, 16)
    x = torch.tensor(np.stack([train[a:a + 24, b:b + 24] for a, b in zip(i, j)]))[:, None]
    y = x + sigma * torch.randn_like(x)
    loss = ((denoise(y) - x) ** 2).mean()                        # squared loss: estimates E[X | Y]
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

psnr = lambda a, b: 10 * np.log10(1.0 / np.mean((a - b) ** 2))
y = test + sigma * rng.standard_normal(test.shape).astype(np.float32)
with torch.no_grad():
    x_cnn = denoise(torch.tensor(y)[None, None])[0, 0].numpy()
best = max((psnr(gaussian_filter(y, s), test), s) for s in [0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 2.0])
print(f"noisy {psnr(y, test):.2f} dB | best Gaussian filter {best[0]:.2f} dB (std {best[1]}) "
      f"| CNN {psnr(x_cnn, test):.2f} dB")
```

Batch normalisation is left out of this small version: with batches of 16 patches its statistics are noisy and, in our runs, it lowered the test PSNR.

### 2.3 Learning without clean images: Noise2Noise

Clean targets are expensive in microscopy, astronomy or low-light photography. A surprising result shows that they are not needed for the squared loss.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Noise2Noise (Lehtinen et al., 2018)]{.tag} Let $Y = X + N$ and $Y' = X + N'$ be two noisy observations of the same image, with $\mathbb{E}[N' \mid X, Y] = 0$ and $\mathbb{E}\|N'\|^2 < \infty$. Then for every function $f$ with $\mathbb{E}\|f(Y)\|^2 < \infty$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|f(Y) - Y'\|^2 = \mathbb{E}\, \|f(Y) - X\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\, \|N'\|^2 .
$$
The two risks differ by a constant, so they have the same minimiser, the MMSE denoiser $\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y]$.

::: proof
Write $f(Y) - Y' = (f(Y) - X) - N'$ and expand the square.

The cross term is $-2\, \mathbb{E} \langle f(Y) - X,\, N' \rangle$. The first factor is a function of $(X, Y)$; conditioning on $(X, Y)$ replaces $N'$ by its conditional mean, which is zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Two caveats matter in practice. With finite data, noisy targets increase the variance of the gradient, so training needs more samples. And the result needs zero-mean noise: for impulse noise, which is not centred, the absolute loss (a median, Proposition 2.2) is the right choice (Exercise 6). Chapter 9 lists the methods that go further and learn from a *single* noisy image per scene.

### 2.4 Super-resolution networks

Super-resolution by a factor $s$ inverts $y = (k * x)\!\downarrow_s + n$. The operator has a kernel of dimension $(1 - 1/s^2)\, n^2$, so the prior does most of the work.

::: def
[Definition 2.6 — SRCNN (Dong, Loy, He and Tang, 2016)]{.tag} The low-resolution image is first upsampled to the target size by bicubic interpolation; three convolutional layers then map it to the high-resolution image:

1.  $9 \times 9$ kernels, 64 channels, ReLU: *patch extraction and representation*;
2.  $1 \times 1$ kernels, 32 channels, ReLU: *non-linear mapping*;
3.  $5 \times 5$ kernels, 1 channel: *reconstruction*.

It is trained with the squared loss on pairs made by downsampling clean images.
:::

The authors read the three layers as the three steps of sparse-coding super-resolution: projecting patches on a low-resolution dictionary, mapping the codes to high-resolution codes, and averaging the overlapping high-resolution patches. The difference is that all three are learned jointly. VDSR (Kim, Lee and Lee, 2016) deepened the network to 20 layers and made it predict the residual between the bicubic image and the target, as DnCNN does for noise.

Upsampling first wastes computation: every layer then works on $s^2$ times more pixels than necessary. The sub-pixel convolution keeps all layers at low resolution.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.7 — Sub-pixel convolution (Shi et al., 2016)]{.tag} Let the last low-resolution layer output $s^2 C$ channels, and let the *periodic shuffle* $\mathrm{PS}$ rearrange them into $C$ channels at resolution $s$ times higher:
$$
\mathrm{PS}(T)_{c,\ s i + a,\ s j + b} = T_{c s^2 + a s + b,\ i,\ j}, \qquad 0 \le a, b < s .
$$

A convolution at low resolution followed by $\mathrm{PS}$ is a transposed convolution of stride $s$ at high resolution. The $s^2$ polyphase components of its high-resolution kernel are the channel slices of the low-resolution kernel.

::: proof
*Sketch.* A high-resolution image is the interleaving of its $s^2$ polyphase components, the low-resolution images $z_{a,b}(i,j) = z(si + a, sj + b)$.

A transposed convolution of stride $s$ inserts $s - 1$ zeros between input pixels and convolves with a kernel $K$.

On the phase $(a, b)$, only the taps of $K$ congruent to $(a, b)$ modulo $s$ meet non-zero inputs. This phase is therefore a low-resolution convolution with the sub-kernel $K_{a,b}$.

Computing the $s^2$ phases as $s^2$ output channels, then interleaving them, is exactly convolution followed by $\mathrm{PS}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

ESPCN, the network of Shi and coauthors, applies this idea and runs in real time on video. In PyTorch the shuffle is `torch.nn.PixelShuffle(s)`.

### 2.5 Losses beyond the squared error

By Proposition 2.2, the loss chooses which summary of the posterior the network returns. Three families are used.

-   **Absolute error.** Many super-resolution networks, EDSR (Lim, Son, Kim, Nah and Lee, 2017) among them, train with the $\ell^1$ loss, which converges better and estimates a median.
-   **Perceptual or feature loss** (Johnson, Alahi and Fei-Fei, 2016). Compare the images through the features $\varphi_j$ of a fixed pretrained classifier, $\|\varphi_j(f_\theta(y)) - \varphi_j(x)\|^2$. Outputs are sharper, with feature-specific artefacts.
-   **Adversarial loss.** A discriminator judges whether the output looks like a natural image (SRGAN, ch. 6.4).

None of these choices is best for every criterion. Chapter 7 proves that accuracy and realism cannot both be optimal.

### 2.6 Pitfalls of end-to-end restoration

The course description asks for a critical look at the methods. Five pitfalls recur in the literature.

1.  **Degradation mismatch.** Benchmarks build low-resolution images with the bicubic kernel. A camera blurs differently, and a network trained on bicubic data over-sharpens or rings on real images. Efrat, Glasner, Apartsin, Nadler and Levin (2013) showed that an accurate blur model matters more than a sophisticated image prior.
2.  **Noise mismatch.** A denoiser trained at one level of Gaussian noise fails at another level, and on real camera noise, which is signal-dependent and spatially correlated after demosaicking.
3.  **Hallucination.** A network trained on faces or textures adds plausible details that were not in the scene. This is acceptable for a photograph and dangerous for a medical or forensic image.
4.  **Benchmark protocol.** Test sets such as Set5, Set14 or BSD100 are small. Whether the PSNR is computed on the luminance channel and whether borders are cropped change results by tenths of a decibel, the size of many claimed improvements.
5.  **Internal versus external learning.** ZSSR (Shocher, Cohen and Irani, 2018) trains a small network on the test image itself, using its self-similarity across scales. The Deep Image Prior (Ulyanov, Vedaldi and Lempitsky, 2018) fits an untrained network to the degraded image and stops early: the architecture alone acts as a prior.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 2
:::

-   A network trained with the squared loss estimates the posterior mean; with the absolute loss, the posterior median. Both blur what is uncertain.
-   DnCNN predicts the noise (residual learning); SRCNN and VDSR learn super-resolution from bicubic-upsampled inputs; sub-pixel convolution works at low resolution.
-   Noise2Noise: noisy targets with zero-mean noise give the same minimiser as clean targets.
-   The weak point of end-to-end methods is the synthetic degradation used to build the training pairs.
::::

## 3. Inverse problems: variational, statistical and hybrid methods {#ch3}

End-to-end networks are trained for one forward model; change the blur or the mask and they must be retrained. The methods of the official theme 2 keep the forward model explicit and use a learned component only as a prior. This chapter sets up the Bayesian framework, the proximal algorithms that solve it, and the plug-and-play methods that insert a denoiser into them.

### 3.1 Bayesian formulation: MAP versus MMSE

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Bayesian inverse problem]{.tag} The prior is $p(x) \propto e^{-\varphi(x)}$, the likelihood of $y = Ax + n$ with Gaussian noise is $p(y \mid x) \propto e^{-\|Ax - y\|^2 / 2\sigma^2}$, and Bayes' rule gives the posterior

$$
p(x \mid y) \propto \exp\!\Big( -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \|Ax - y\|^2 - \varphi(x) \Big).
$$

The MAP estimator minimises the exponent (a variational problem, Definition 0.6). The MMSE estimator is the mean of the posterior, an integral in dimension $|\Omega|$ that requires sampling.
:::

The two are often confused. The next proposition shows they behave differently even in dimension one.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — MAP and MMSE under a Laplace prior]{.tag} Let $p(x) \propto e^{-|x|/\beta}$ and $y = x + n$ with $n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. Then:

-   the MAP estimator is the soft thresholding at level $\lambda = \sigma^2 / \beta$: it is *exactly zero* on $[-\lambda, \lambda]$;
-   the MMSE estimator is a smooth, odd function of $y$ that is non-zero for every $y \neq 0$.

::: proof
The MAP minimises $\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(x - y)^2 + |x|/\beta$; multiplying by $\sigma^2$ gives Proposition 1.8 with $\lambda = \sigma^2/\beta$.

For the MMSE, take $y > 0$ and compare the posterior at $x > 0$ and at $-x$. The prior is symmetric, and the likelihood ratio is
$$
\frac{p(x \mid y)}{p(-x \mid y)} = \exp\!\Big( \frac{2 x y}{\sigma^2} \Big) > 1 .
$$
The posterior puts more mass on positive values, so $\mathbb{E}[X \mid y] > 0$. Oddness follows from symmetry, and smoothness from differentiation under the integral sign. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The same gap appears in images. The MAP of the TV prior is piecewise constant, which causes staircasing, whereas its posterior mean is not: Louchet and Moisan (2013) showed that the posterior expectation of the TV model avoids staircasing. Exercise 7 computes both estimators numerically.

### 3.2 Proximal operators and ADMM

::: def
[Definition 3.3 — Proximal operator]{.tag} For a proper, convex, lower semicontinuous $g$ and $\tau > 0$,
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\tau g}(v) = \arg\min_x\ \tfrac12 \|x - v\|^2 + \tau\, g(x).
$$
The minimiser exists and is unique, and $\mathrm{prox}_{\tau g}$ is firmly non-expansive.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — A proximal operator is a MAP denoiser]{.tag} If $v = x + \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)$ and the prior is $e^{-\varphi}$, the MAP estimate of $x$ is
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\sigma^2 \varphi}(v).
$$

This is Definition 0.6 with $A = I$, multiplied by $\sigma^2$. Soft thresholding and the ROF model of ch. 1 are examples.
:::

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.5 — ADMM in scaled form]{.tag} To minimise $f(x) + g(v)$ under the constraint $x = v$, with a penalty parameter $\rho > 0$, iterate:

1.  $x^{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{f/\rho}(v^k - u^k)$;
2.  $v^{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{g/\rho}(x^{k+1} + u^k)$;
3.  $u^{k+1} = u^k + x^{k+1} - v^{k+1}$.

For closed proper convex $f$ and $g$ whose Lagrangian has a saddle point, the iterates converge to a solution for every $\rho > 0$ (Eckstein and Bertsekas, 1992; Boyd, Parikh, Chu, Peleato and Eckstein, 2011).
:::

For deblurring, $f(x) = \frac12 \|k * x - y\|^2$ and the first step is a Fourier division:
$$
x^{k+1} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\Big[ \frac{\overline{\hat k}\, \hat y + \rho\, \mathcal{F}(v^k - u^k)}{|\hat k|^2 + \rho} \Big].
$$
The second step, with $g = \lambda \varphi$, is a MAP denoising of $x^{k+1} + u^k$ at noise level $\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda / \rho}$, by Proposition 3.4.

### 3.3 Plug-and-play ADMM and its convergence

Venkatakrishnan, Bouman and Wohlberg (2013) observed that the prior only enters ADMM through a denoiser. They replaced step 2 by *any* denoiser: BM3D, non-local means, and later a CNN. The forward model stays explicit, so one denoiser serves deblurring, super-resolution and inpainting alike.

::: thm
[Algorithm 3.6 — Plug-and-play ADMM with continuation (Chan, Wang and Elgendy, 2017)]{.tag} Let $D_\sigma$ be a denoiser for noise level $\sigma$, and fix $\lambda > 0$, $\rho_0 > 0$, $\gamma > 1$. Iterate:

1.  $x^{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{f/\rho_k}(v^k - u^k)$;
2.  $v^{k+1} = D_{\sigma_k}(x^{k+1} + u^k)$ with $\sigma_k = \sqrt{\lambda / \rho_k}$;
3.  $u^{k+1} = u^k + x^{k+1} - v^{k+1}$;
4.  $\rho_{k+1} = \gamma \rho_k$.

Chan and coauthors increase $\rho$ only when the residual has not decreased enough; the geometric version above is the simplest case.
:::

A denoiser is generally not a proximal operator, so the convex theory of ADMM no longer applies. Chan and coauthors replace it by a weak assumption.

::: def
[Definition 3.7 — Bounded denoiser]{.tag} A family $(D_\sigma)_{\sigma > 0}$ of maps of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a *bounded denoiser* if there is a constant $C$, independent of $n$ and $\sigma$, such that
$$
\|D_\sigma(v) - v\|^2 \le n\, C\, \sigma^2 \qquad \text{for all } v \in \mathbb{R}^n .
$$
A denoiser that moves each pixel by at most a multiple of the noise level satisfies it.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.8 — Fixed-point convergence of PnP-ADMM (Chan, Wang and Elgendy, 2017)]{.tag} Assume $f$ is differentiable with $\|\nabla f(x)\| \le L \sqrt{n}$ for all $x$, and $D$ is a bounded denoiser. Then the iterates of Algorithm 3.6 satisfy
$$
x^k \to x^\star, \qquad v^k \to x^\star, \qquad u^k \to 0
$$
for some $x^\star \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

::: proof
Write $\rho_k = \gamma^k \rho_0$. Each step contributes one bound.

1.  *Step 1.* The optimality condition of the proximal step is $\nabla f(x^{k+1}) + \rho_k (x^{k+1} - v^k + u^k) = 0$, so
    $$
    \|x^{k+1} - v^k + u^k\| \le L \sqrt{n} / \rho_k .
    $$
2.  *Steps 2 and 3.* By step 3, $u^{k+1} = (x^{k+1} + u^k) - v^{k+1}$, the move of the denoiser. Definition 3.7 with $\sigma_k^2 = \lambda / \rho_k$ gives
    $$
    \|u^{k+1}\| \le \sqrt{n C \lambda / \rho_k} .
    $$
3.  *Increments.* Write $v^{k+1} - v^k = (x^{k+1} - v^k) - (u^{k+1} - u^k)$, and bound $x^{k+1} - v^k$ by bounds 1 and 2. All terms are $O(\rho_{k-1}^{-1/2})$, so $\|v^{k+1} - v^k\| \le M \gamma^{-k/2}$ for a constant $M$.
4.  *Conclusion.* The series of the $\gamma^{-k/2}$ converges, so $(v^k)$ is a Cauchy sequence with a limit $x^\star$. By bound 2, $u^k \to 0$; then by bound 1, $x^{k+1} - v^k \to 0$, so $x^k \to x^\star$ as well. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The gradient bound holds for a quadratic data term on a bounded set of images, such as $[0, 1]^n$, which is how the theorem is applied.

::: note
[Remark 3.9 — What the theorem does not say]{.tag} The convergence comes from the vanishing steps: as $\rho_k \to \infty$, the denoiser is asked to remove less and less noise and eventually does almost nothing. The limit depends on $\rho_0$ and $\gamma$, and it is not shown to minimise any objective or to be close to the true image.

Stronger guarantees need stronger denoisers. Ryu, Liu, Wang, Chen, Wang and Yin (2019) prove convergence for a fixed $\rho$ when the residual $D - I$ is Lipschitz with a small constant, a property they enforce by spectral normalisation. Hurault, Leclaire and Papadakis (2022) train a *gradient-step denoiser* $D = I - \nabla g_\theta$, which turns plug-and-play into a proximal-gradient method on an explicit, non-convex objective.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.10 — Plug-and-play deblurring]{.tag} On the problem of Example 1.6 (Gaussian blur of standard deviation 2, noise $0.01$), the code below runs Algorithm 3.6 with the TV denoiser of Definition 1.7, solved by Chambolle's algorithm, with $\lambda = 2 \times 10^{-4}$, $\rho_0 = 10^{-3}$ and $\gamma = 1.2$.

After 30 iterations it reaches 21.24 dB, against 20.74 dB for Tikhonov and 21.04 dB for the oracle Wiener filter. The increments $\|v^{k+1} - v^k\|$ are divided by about 5 every 10 iterations, close to the factor $1.2^{10} \approx 6.2$ of the continuation, which is the mechanism of Theorem 3.8.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_sample_image

def grad(u):                                   # forward differences, Neumann boundary
    gx, gy = np.zeros_like(u), np.zeros_like(u)
    gx[:-1] = u[1:] - u[:-1]; gy[:, :-1] = u[:, 1:] - u[:, :-1]
    return gx, gy

def div(px, py):                               # div = -grad^T
    dx, dy = px.copy(), py.copy()
    dx[1:] -= px[:-1]; dx[-1] = -px[-2]
    dy[:, 1:] -= py[:, :-1]; dy[:, -1] = -py[:, -2]
    return dx + dy

def tv_denoise(f, t, iters=50):                # prox of t*TV, Chambolle (2004) dual projection
    px, py = np.zeros_like(f), np.zeros_like(f)
    for _ in range(iters):
        gx, gy = grad(div(px, py) - f / t)
        nrm = 1 + 0.125 * np.sqrt(gx ** 2 + gy ** 2)
        px, py = (px + 0.125 * gx) / nrm, (py + 0.125 * gy) / nrm
    return f - t * div(px, py)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = load_sample_image("china.jpg").mean(axis=2)[100:356, 200:456] / 255.0
f = np.fft.fftfreq(256)
K = np.exp(-2 * np.pi ** 2 * 2.0 ** 2 * (f[:, None] ** 2 + f[None, :] ** 2))
blur = lambda u: np.real(np.fft.ifft2(K * np.fft.fft2(u)))
y = blur(x) + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
psnr = lambda u: 10 * np.log10(1.0 / np.mean((u - x) ** 2))

def pnp_admm(y, denoise, lam=2e-4, rho=1e-3, gamma=1.2, iters=30):
    """Plug-and-play ADMM for 0.5 * ||k * x - y||^2 + lam * prior, with continuation on rho."""
    Ky = np.conj(K) * np.fft.fft2(y)
    v, u = y.copy(), np.zeros_like(y)
    for it in range(iters):
        x_k = np.real(np.fft.ifft2((Ky + rho * np.fft.fft2(v - u)) / (np.abs(K) ** 2 + rho)))
        v_old, v = v, denoise(x_k + u, lam / rho)       # the prior acts only through a denoiser
        u = u + x_k - v
        rho *= gamma                                      # continuation (Chan, Wang and Elgendy, 2017)
        if it % 10 == 9:
            print(f"iteration {it + 1}: PSNR {psnr(v):.2f} dB, |v - v_old| = {np.linalg.norm(v - v_old):.4f}, "
                  f"|u| = {np.linalg.norm(u):.4f}")
    return v

print(f"blurred {psnr(y):.2f} dB")
x_hat = pnp_admm(y, tv_denoise)
```

The TV denoiser is called with the parameter $\lambda / \rho_k$, the weight of the TV term, which plays the role of $\sigma_k^2$. Replacing `tv_denoise` by a trained CNN, such as the network of ch. 2, gives the deep plug-and-play methods; DPIR (Zhang, Li, Zuo, Zhang, Van Gool and Timofte, 2022) is a widely used instance.

### 3.4 Denoisers are scores: Tweedie's formula and RED

Plug-and-play uses a denoiser as a black box. Tweedie's formula says what an *optimal* denoiser computes, and it is the key to ch. 8.

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.11 — Tweedie's formula]{.tag} Let $Y = X + \sigma Z$ with $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ independent of $X$, and let $p_\sigma$ be the density of $Y$. Then
$$
\mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] = y + \sigma^2\, \nabla \log p_\sigma(y).
$$

::: proof
Let $g_\sigma$ be the Gaussian density of $\sigma Z$, so that $p_\sigma(y) = \int p_X(x)\, g_\sigma(y - x)\, dx$. The Gaussian satisfies
$$
\nabla_y\, g_\sigma(y - x) = -\frac{y - x}{\sigma^2}\, g_\sigma(y - x).
$$

Differentiating under the integral sign,
$$
\sigma^2\, \nabla p_\sigma(y) = \int (x - y)\, p_X(x)\, g_\sigma(y - x)\, dx = p_\sigma(y)\, \big( \mathbb{E}[X \mid Y = y] - y \big).
$$
Divide by $p_\sigma(y)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The formula goes back to Robbins (1956); Efron (2011) revived it. Read backwards, it turns the residual of an MMSE denoiser $D_\sigma$ into the *score* of the noisy image distribution:

::: key
[Key result — a denoiser gives the score]{.tag}
$$
\nabla \log p_\sigma(y) = \frac{D_\sigma(y) - y}{\sigma^2}
$$
:::

The code below checks the formula on a one-dimensional mixture prior, where both sides can be computed independently.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

w, mu, s = np.array([0.3, 0.7]), np.array([-2.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.5, 0.8])  # prior: 2-Gaussian mixture
sigma = 0.7                                                                 # noise level
xs = np.linspace(-8, 8, 20001)
prior = (w * norm.pdf(xs[:, None], mu, s)).sum(axis=1)

def posterior_mean(y):                                   # E[X | Y=y] by brute-force integration
    post = prior * norm.pdf(y, xs, sigma)
    return (xs * post).sum() / post.sum()

def tweedie(y):                                          # y + sigma^2 d/dy log p_Y(y)
    sd = np.sqrt(s ** 2 + sigma ** 2)                    # p_Y is again a Gaussian mixture
    p = w * norm.pdf(y, mu, sd)
    dp = (p * (mu - y) / sd ** 2).sum()
    return y + sigma ** 2 * dp / p.sum()

for y in [-3.0, -0.5, 0.5, 2.5]:
    print(f"y = {y:+.1f}:  integration {posterior_mean(y):+.4f}   Tweedie {tweedie(y):+.4f}")
```

Both columns agree to four decimals: for instance $-2.3345$ at $y = -3$ and $+0.7007$ at $y = 0.5$.

::: def
[Definition 3.12 — Regularisation by denoising (Romano, Elad and Milanfar, 2017)]{.tag} RED defines the regulariser $\rho(x) = \frac12 x^\top (x - D(x))$ and solves $\min_x f(x) + \lambda \rho(x)$ by gradient steps
$$
x \leftarrow x - \mu \big( \nabla f(x) + \lambda (x - D(x)) \big),
$$
relying on the identity $\nabla \rho(x) = x - D(x)$.
:::

That identity needs the denoiser to be locally homogeneous with a symmetric Jacobian. Reehorst and Schniter (2019) showed that practical denoisers violate these conditions, so RED does not minimise the stated objective. Tweedie's formula gives a cleaner reading: if $D = D_\sigma$ is the MMSE denoiser, then $x - D_\sigma(x) = -\sigma^2 \nabla \log p_\sigma(x)$, and RED is a gradient descent on $f - \lambda \sigma^2 \log p_\sigma$, a MAP with the *smoothed* prior.

### 3.5 Unrolled networks and the hybrid spectrum

::: def
[Definition 3.13 — Algorithm unrolling (Gregor and LeCun, 2010)]{.tag} Fix a number $K$ of iterations of an algorithm, for example ISTA,
$$
x^{k+1} = \mathrm{soft}_{\lambda \eta}\big( x^k - \eta A^\top (A x^k - y) \big),
$$
and make its step sizes, matrices and thresholds learnable. The result is a $K$-layer network trained end-to-end on pairs; for ISTA it is called LISTA.
:::

Unrolled networks embed the forward model in their architecture and need few parameters, but they are trained for the operator $A$ used during training. The table summarises the spectrum from ch. 1 to ch. 3.

| Method | Forward model at test time | Training data | Guarantees |
|---|---|---|---|
| Variational (ch. 1) | explicit, any $A$ | none | convex: global minimum |
| Plug-and-play (ch. 3.3) | explicit, any $A$ | clean images for the denoiser | fixed point under assumptions |
| Unrolled (ch. 3.5) | built into the layers | pairs for one $A$ | few |
| End-to-end (ch. 2) | implicit, fixed $A$ | pairs for one $A$ | none beyond Proposition 2.2 |

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 3
:::

-   MAP is a variational problem; MMSE is a posterior integral. They differ as soon as the prior is non-Gaussian.
-   A proximal operator is a MAP denoiser; ADMM alternates a data step and a denoising step.
-   Plug-and-play replaces the denoising step by any denoiser; with continuation and a bounded denoiser, the iterates converge, though not to a characterised point.
-   Tweedie: an MMSE denoiser gives the score of the noisy distribution. This reinterprets RED and powers ch. 8.
::::

## 4. Generative models for texture synthesis {#ch4}

Synthesis asks for new images that look like a given one without copying it. Textures are the natural first case, and the subject of the official theme 3: they are stationary, so a model can be estimated from a single exemplar. This chapter goes from Gaussian models to the statistics of convolutional networks, and shows what each one keeps and loses.

### 4.1 Textures as stationary random fields

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Stationary random field and texture synthesis]{.tag} A random image $U$ on $\Omega$ (periodic) is *stationary* if $\tau_a U$ has the same law as $U$ for every translation $a$.

*Exemplar-based texture synthesis* estimates a stationary model from one image $u$, then draws samples that should be perceived as the same texture while differing from $u$.
:::

Two failure modes bound the problem: a model that is too poor produces samples that do not look like $u$, and a model that is too rich reproduces $u$ itself, possibly shifted. Julesz (1962) conjectured that textures with the same second-order statistics are indistinguishable; the conjecture is false, but it started the search for the right statistics.

Heeger and Bergen (1995) matched the histograms of the subbands of a wavelet pyramid. Portilla and Simoncelli (2000) matched a set of joint statistics of complex wavelet coefficients, a model that was the reference for a decade. Efros and Leung (1999) took a non-parametric route: grow the image pixel by pixel, copying a pixel from a place of the exemplar whose neighbourhood matches. It produces striking results but tends to copy whole regions verbatim.

### 4.2 Gaussian textures and random phase noise

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Spot noise and random phase noise (Galerne, Gousseau and Morel, 2011)]{.tag} Let $u$ be the exemplar, $m$ its mean, $|\Omega|$ its number of pixels and
$$
t = \frac{u - m}{\sqrt{|\Omega|}} .
$$

-   The *asymptotic discrete spot noise* is $\mathrm{ADSN}(u) = m + t * W$, with $W$ a standard Gaussian white noise on $\Omega$.
-   The *random phase noise* $\mathrm{RPN}(u)$ keeps the Fourier modulus $|\hat u|$ and replaces the phase by a uniform random phase, symmetrised so that the image is real.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.3 — ADSN reproduces the empirical covariance]{.tag} $\mathrm{ADSN}(u)$ is a stationary Gaussian field with mean $m$ and covariance
$$
\mathrm{Cov}\big(V(x), V(y)\big) = \sum_{z \in \Omega} t(z)\, t(z + y - x) ,
$$
the empirical autocovariance of $u$ at the shift $y - x$. Equivalently, for $\omega \neq 0$, $\mathbb{E}|\hat V(\omega)|^2 = |\hat u(\omega)|^2$.

::: proof
$V(x) - m = \sum_z t(z) W(x - z)$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, hence Gaussian and centred.

Its covariance is $\sum_{z, z'} t(z) t(z')\, \mathbb{E}[W(x - z) W(y - z')]$. The expectation is $1$ when $x - z = y - z'$, that is $z' = z + y - x$, and $0$ otherwise.

The result only depends on $y - x$, which is stationarity. The spectral form follows from Theorem 0.2: $\hat V(\omega) = \hat t(\omega) \hat W(\omega)$ and $\mathbb{E}|\hat W(\omega)|^2 = |\Omega|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

RPN differs from ADSN only by the random modulus of the noise; both are fast (one FFT) and both are exactly right for *micro-textures* such as sand, plaster or fabric. They fail on textures made of objects, such as bricks, pebbles or leaves, because the geometry of an image is carried by the phase of its Fourier transform. Oppenheim and Lim (1981) illustrated this: swapping the phases of two images swaps what we recognise.

### 4.3 Gram matrices of convolutional features

Gatys, Ecker and Bethge (2015) replaced hand-designed statistics by those of a convolutional network trained for classification.

::: def
[Definition 4.4 — Gram matrix of a layer]{.tag} Let $F^l(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{C_l \times M_l}$ be the feature maps of layer $l$ of a fixed network ($C_l$ channels, $M_l$ positions). Its *Gram matrix* is
$$
G^l(x) = \frac{1}{M_l}\, F^l(x)\, F^l(x)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{C_l \times C_l} .
$$

The *texture loss* compares an image $x$ with the exemplar $u$ over a set of layers,
$$
\mathcal{L}(x) = \sum_l w_l\, \big\| G^l(x) - G^l(u) \big\|_F^2 .
$$
Synthesis starts from white noise and minimises $\mathcal{L}$ by L-BFGS, with gradients obtained by backpropagation.
:::

The paper uses the layers of VGG-19 at several depths. The deeper the layers included, the larger the structures reproduced.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.5 — Gram matrices are stationary statistics]{.tag} If the feature extractor is fully convolutional with periodic padding, then for every translation $a$,
$$
G^l(\tau_a x) = G^l(x) .
$$
Each entry $G^l_{ij}(x)$ is the spatial average of $F^l_i F^l_j$, an estimator of $\mathbb{E}[F^l_i(U)(p)\, F^l_j(U)(p)]$ when $U$ is stationary.

::: proof
By Proposition 0.8, $F^l(\tau_a x) = \tau_a F^l(x)$: translating the image translates every feature map. A sum over all positions is invariant under a translation of its terms. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The averaging is the strength and the weakness of the model. It makes the statistics independent of position, as a texture model should be, but it also forgets *where* things are relative to each other beyond the receptive field. Long-range regularity, such as the alignment of bricks or a periodic grid, is weakly constrained. Ustyuzhaninov, Brendel, Gatys and Bethge (2017) showed that even random, untrained convolutional filters at several scales give convincing textures: much of the model lies in the Gram statistics rather than in the trained weights.

### 4.4 The spectrum constraint

Liu, Gousseau and Xia (2016) combined the two models of this chapter: Gram matrices for local structure, and the Fourier modulus of random phase noise for long-range regularity.

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — Projection on a Fourier modulus]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{A}_u$ be the set of images whose Fourier modulus equals $|\hat u|$. For an image $x$ whose DFT never vanishes, the closest point of $\mathcal{A}_u$ to $x$ is
$$
P(x) = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\Big( |\hat u|\, \frac{\hat x}{|\hat x|} \Big),
$$
the image with the modulus of $u$ and the phase of $x$.

::: proof
By Parseval,
$$
\|x - z\|^2 = |\Omega|^{-1} \sum_\omega |\hat x(\omega) - \hat z(\omega)|^2 ,
$$
and the constraint fixes $|\hat z(\omega)| = |\hat u(\omega)|$ frequency by frequency.

For a fixed modulus $r$, the distance $|\hat x(\omega) - r e^{i\psi}|$ is minimal when $\psi$ is the argument of $\hat x(\omega)$. This choice respects the Hermitian symmetry of $\hat x$, so $P(x)$ is real. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The synthesis then minimises $\mathcal{L}(x) + \beta\, \|x - P(x)\|^2$. The gradient of $\frac12 \mathrm{dist}(x, \mathcal{A}_u)^2$ is $x - P(x)$ wherever the projection is unique, so in practice $P(x)$ is computed and held fixed during the backward pass.

::: ex
[Example 4.7 — Gram statistics lose the spectrum]{.tag} The code below synthesises a $64 \times 64$ periodic texture, a grid of blobs plus fine noise, with the Gram matrices of random filters at four scales. Without the spectrum term the Gram loss is driven to about $10^{-6}$, yet the Fourier modulus stays far from the exemplar's, with a relative error of about $1.25$. With $\beta = 1$ the relative error drops to about $0.001$, while the Gram loss stays of order $10^{-6}$: the two constraints are compatible, and the second one is not implied by the first.
:::

```python
import numpy as np, torch
torch.manual_seed(0); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# Exemplar: a 64 x 64 periodic texture (a grid of blobs) + fine noise
n = 64
i, j = np.mgrid[:n, :n]
u = sum(np.exp(-((i - a) ** 2 + (j - b) ** 2) / 6.0)
        for a in range(4, n, 8) for b in range(4, n, 8))
u = u + 0.1 * rng.standard_normal((n, n))

# 1. Random phase noise (Galerne, Gousseau and Morel, 2011): keep |FFT|, draw the phase
theta = np.angle(np.fft.fft2(rng.standard_normal((n, n))))       # phase of a white noise (symmetric)
rpn = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.abs(np.fft.fft2(u)) * np.exp(1j * theta)))
print("RPN: max modulus error", np.abs(np.abs(np.fft.fft2(rpn)) - np.abs(np.fft.fft2(u))).max().round(10))

# 2. Gram-matrix synthesis with random convolutional features (+ optional spectrum term)
convs = [torch.nn.Conv2d(1, 32, k, padding=k // 2, padding_mode="circular") for k in (3, 5, 7, 11)]
def grams(x):
    out = []
    for c in convs:
        F = torch.relu(c(x)).flatten(2)[0]                 # 32 x (n*n) feature maps
        out.append(F @ F.T / F.shape[1])
    return out
U = torch.tensor(u, dtype=torch.float32)[None, None]
with torch.no_grad():
    G_u, mod_u = grams(U), torch.fft.fft2(U).abs()

def spectrum_projection(x):                               # closest image with the exemplar's modulus
    X = torch.fft.fft2(x)
    return torch.real(torch.fft.ifft2(mod_u * X / (X.abs() + 1e-8)))

def synthesize(beta):
    x = torch.randn(1, 1, n, n).requires_grad_()
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([x], max_iter=150)
    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = sum(((g - h) ** 2).sum() for g, h in zip(grams(x), G_u))
        if beta > 0:
            loss = loss + beta * ((x - spectrum_projection(x).detach()) ** 2).mean()
        loss.backward()
        return loss
    opt.step(closure)
    return x.detach()

for beta in (0.0, 1.0):
    x = synthesize(beta)
    gram = sum(((g - h) ** 2).sum() for g, h in zip(grams(x), G_u)).item()
    spec = ((torch.fft.fft2(x).abs() - mod_u) ** 2).mean().sqrt().item() / mod_u.mean().item()
    print(f"beta = {beta}: Gram loss {gram:.2e}, relative spectrum error {spec:.3f}")
```

### 4.5 Feed-forward texture networks and style transfer

Optimising each sample from noise takes many gradient steps per image. Ulyanov, Lebedev, Vedaldi and Lempitsky (2016) and Johnson, Alahi and Fei-Fei (2016) instead train a generator $g_\theta$ to minimise $\mathbb{E}_z\, \mathcal{L}(g_\theta(z))$: once trained, a sample costs a single forward pass.

The catch is diversity. The loss is minimised by one good image, and nothing forces different $z$ to give different textures. Ulyanov, Vedaldi and Lempitsky (2017) added a term that rewards diversity across a batch.

*Style transfer* (Gatys, Ecker and Bethge, 2016) mixes two images: the content $c$ through a deep feature map, the style $s$ through Gram matrices,
$$
\min_x\ \alpha\, \|F^{l_0}(x) - F^{l_0}(c)\|^2 + \beta \sum_l w_l\, \|G^l(x) - G^l(s)\|_F^2 .
$$

### 4.6 A critical look

-   **Copy versus innovation.** The exemplar and all its translates minimise $\mathcal{L}$ exactly. A synthesis may converge to a shifted copy, which a simple nearest-patch distance to the exemplar reveals.
-   **Stationarity.** Exemplars with a gradient of scale or lighting violate the model; Gram averaging mixes regions that should stay apart.
-   **Evaluation.** There is no ground truth. Papers rely on visual inspection and user studies, or on statistics computed by yet another network, which favours methods built on the same features.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Key takeaways — chapter 4
:::

-   A texture is a stationary random field; synthesis samples from a model estimated on one exemplar.
-   ADSN and RPN reproduce the power spectrum exactly and fail on geometric textures, whose structure is in the phase.
-   Gatys' Gram matrices are translation-invariant statistics of convolutional features; they capture local structure and lose long-range arrangement.
-   The spectrum constraint of Liu, Gousseau and Xia projects on the exemplar's Fourier modulus and restores regularity.
::::

## 5. Autoencoders and variational autoencoders {#ch5}

Texture models describe one stationary image. To generate natural images of a whole class, such as faces or digits, we need a model of a distribution on a high-dimensional space whose samples concentrate near a low-dimensional set. Autoencoders learn such a set; variational autoencoders, the official theme 4, turn it into a probabilistic generative model.

### 5.1 Autoencoders and what they encode

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Autoencoder]{.tag} An *encoder* $E : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^d$ and a *decoder* $G : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^n$, with $d < n$, are trained to minimise the reconstruction error
$$
\mathbb{E}\, \|G(E(X)) - X\|^2 .
$$
The code $z = E(x)$ is a compressed representation; the image of $G$ is a $d$-dimensional set that should contain the data.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Linear autoencoders compute PCA (Baldi and Hornik, 1989)]{.tag} Let $X$ be centred with covariance $\Sigma$, of eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n$. Over linear maps $E$ and $G$,
$$
\min_{E, G}\ \mathbb{E}\, \|G E X - X\|^2 = \sum_{i > d} \lambda_i ,
$$
attained when $G E$ is the orthogonal projection onto the span of the top $d$ eigenvectors.

::: proof
The product $M = G E$ has rank at most $d$. Once its range $V$ is fixed, the best such map is the orthogonal projection $P_V$, which sends each point to its closest point in the range.

Then
$$
\mathbb{E}\|X - P_V X\|^2 = \mathrm{tr}\, \Sigma - \mathrm{tr}(P_V \Sigma).
$$
By Ky Fan's maximum principle, $\mathrm{tr}(P_V \Sigma)$ over projections of rank $d$ is at most $\lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_d$, with equality for the top eigenvectors. Any factorisation $M = G E$ through $\mathbb{R}^d$ realises it. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Non-linear autoencoders can do much better when the data lie on a *curved* low-dimensional set. Newson, Almansa, Gousseau and Ladjal (2018) chose the simplest such set to dissect autoencoders: images of centred disks, a family with a single parameter, the radius. They studied how the encoder and the decoder represent this one-dimensional family, and how well the network interpolates to radii absent from the training set.

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Disks: one parameter, many principal components]{.tag} The code below builds 400 anti-aliased disks of radius between 2 and 14 pixels on a $32 \times 32$ grid and computes their principal components. The share of the variance explained by the first $k$ components is:

-   $k = 1$: 67.2 %;
-   $k = 2$: 83.0 %;
-   $k = 5$: 95.4 %;
-   $k = 10$: 99.2 %.

Yet a non-linear code of dimension 1 is exact: encode the area $z = \sum_p x(p)$, and decode the disk of area $z$. A linear model needs about ten dimensions for what a curved one does with one.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

n = 32
yy, xx = np.mgrid[:n, :n] - (n - 1) / 2                  # pixel coordinates, centred
rho = np.sqrt(xx ** 2 + yy ** 2)
radii = np.linspace(2, 14, 400)                           # a one-parameter family of images
disks = np.clip(radii[:, None, None] - rho[None] + 0.5, 0, 1).reshape(400, -1)   # anti-aliased disks
centred = disks - disks.mean(0)
lam = np.linalg.svd(centred, compute_uv=False) ** 2       # PCA spectrum
ratio = np.cumsum(lam) / lam.sum()
for k in (1, 2, 5, 10, 20):
    print(f"{k:2d} principal components explain {100 * ratio[k - 1]:.1f} % of the variance")
```

### 5.2 Latent variable models

An autoencoder does not generate: decoding a random code gives garbage if the codes of the data occupy a small, irregular part of $\mathbb{R}^d$. A latent variable model fixes the distribution of the codes in advance.

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Deep latent variable model]{.tag} Draw $z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I_d)$, then $x \sim p_\theta(x \mid z)$, for instance $\mathcal{N}(G_\theta(z), \sigma^2 I)$ or independent Bernoulli pixels with means $G_\theta(z)$. The model density is
$$
p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz .
$$
:::

Maximum likelihood would maximise $\sum_i \log p_\theta(x_i)$, but the integral has no closed form when $G_\theta$ is a network, and neither has the posterior $p_\theta(z \mid x)$. Variational inference replaces the posterior by an approximation $q_\phi(z \mid x)$ computed by an encoder.

### 5.3 The evidence lower bound

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Evidence lower bound]{.tag} For every density $q(z \mid x)$ with the same support as the posterior,
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z \mid x)\, \|\, p(z)\big)}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(\theta, q;\, x)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q(z \mid x)\, \|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big).
$$
Since a Kullback–Leibler divergence is non-negative, $\log p_\theta(x) \ge \mathrm{ELBO}$, with equality if and only if $q$ is the true posterior.

::: proof
The quantity $\log p_\theta(x)$ does not depend on $z$, so it equals its expectation under $q$. Bayes' rule gives $p_\theta(x) = p_\theta(x, z) / p_\theta(z \mid x)$; multiply and divide by $q(z \mid x)$ inside the logarithm:
$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \mathbb{E}_q\Big[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z \mid x)}\Big] + \mathbb{E}_q\Big[\log \frac{q(z \mid x)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)}\Big].
$$
The second term is the KL to the posterior. In the first, write $p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x \mid z) p(z)$ to obtain the two terms of the ELBO. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The ELBO has a direct reading: a *reconstruction* term, which asks the decoder to explain $x$ from codes drawn by the encoder, and a *regularisation* term, which keeps the encoder's distribution close to the prior so that random codes decode to plausible images.

### 5.4 The reparameterisation trick and the Gaussian KL

The variational autoencoder (Kingma and Welling, 2014; Rezende, Mohamed and Wierstra, 2014) uses a Gaussian encoder with mean $\mu_\phi(x)$ and diagonal covariance $\mathrm{diag}\, \sigma^2_\phi(x)$, and maximises the ELBO jointly in $\theta$ and $\phi$ by stochastic gradients.

::: prop
[Proposition 5.6 — Reparameterisation]{.tag} Write $z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$. For a differentiable $h$,
$$
\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[h(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\varepsilon}\big[ \nabla_\phi\, h\big(\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon\big) \big].
$$

The law of $\varepsilon$ does not depend on $\phi$, so the gradient passes inside the expectation. A single draw of $\varepsilon$ gives an unbiased estimate, with a much smaller variance in practice than the score-function estimator.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 5.7 — KL between a diagonal Gaussian and the standard Gaussian]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \mathrm{diag}\, \sigma^2)\, \|\, \mathcal{N}(0, I)\big) = \frac12 \sum_{j=1}^d \big( \mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2 \big).
